blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — bed-exit alarms and fall prevention
stem: A family member asks whether a bed-exit alarm physically keeps a high-risk client in bed. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: The alarm notifies staff when the client begins to exit the bed; it does not physically prevent bed exit and is only one possible part of an individualized fall plan.
options.B: The alarm restrains the client by locking the bed surface until a staff member responds, so other fall-prevention measures are usually unnecessary.
options.C: The alarm prevents voluntary bed exit by automatically raising or locking side rails whenever the client begins to move toward the edge of the bed.
options.D: The alarm eliminates fall risk once activated because staff are guaranteed to reach the client before the client can leave the bed.

rationale: A is correct. AHRQ describes bed alarms as devices that notify staff when a patient attempts to get out of bed. Current AHRQ fall-prevention resources emphasize formal risk assessment and a tailored, multifactorial prevention plan rather than reliance on one device. Bed alarms do not mechanically restrain a client or guarantee staff will intervene before bed exit. B, C, and D incorrectly describe physical restraint or complete prevention.
educational_objective: Explain that bed-exit alarms are alerting tools rather than physical restraints and should be considered only within an individualized fall-prevention plan when appropriate.
source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ); NCSBN
source_document_title: Fall TIPS: A Patient-Centered Fall Prevention Toolkit; Falls — PSNet; Another Fall; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: Current AHRQ Fall TIPS and PSNet fall-prevention resources live-rechecked 2026-08-21; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: AHRQ Fall TIPS: fall prevention uses formal risk assessment, a personalized prevention plan, and consistent execution. AHRQ PSNet Falls: successful programs use individualized combinations of strategies, including technological interventions such as bed alarms. AHRQ Another Fall: bed alarms notify staff when a patient attempts to get out of bed.
source_claim_supported: AHRQ directly supports that bed alarms alert staff to attempted bed exit and that fall prevention should be individualized and multifactorial rather than relying on alarms as a complete prevention strategy.
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p.8: protect clients from injury, assess the care environment, and educate clients/families on safety concerns.
pdf_visual_verification: PASS — official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Safety and Infection Prevention and Control page was screenshot-verified earlier in this continuation; fall-prevention claims rely on current AHRQ HTML.

option_audit.A: Correct; accurately describes alerting rather than physical restraint and places the device within individualized prevention.
option_audit.B: Plausible misconception but bed alarms do not lock the client in bed and do not replace other measures.
option_audit.C: Plausible equipment misconception but bed-exit alarms do not automatically raise or lock rails.
option_audit.D: Plausible reassurance misconception but an alarm does not eliminate risk or guarantee rescue before exit.

cueing_audit.answer_length: All options are comparable in detail and clinical framing; the key is not uniquely signaled by length.
cueing_audit.absolute_words: No distractor depends on simplistic always/never/only wording.
